v: Calgary was almost called Fort Brisebois.
In eighteen seventy-five, the North-West Mounted Police built a fort where the Elbow River meets the Bow.
At first, it was simply called The Elbow.
By January eighteen seventy-six, the officer in charge, Inspector Éphrem Brisebois, had named it after himself.
His men and the local settlers disliked the name.
Assistant Commissioner Acheson Irvine cancelled the order. On February twenty-ninth, eighteen seventy-six, he wrote to Ottawa.
Colonel Macleod, he wrote, had supported the name of Calgary, which Irvine believed meant clear running water.
James Macleod took the name from one of his favourite places: Calgary, on the Isle of Mull, in Scotland.
It's a broad, sandy bay on the island's west coast, with a castle on the hillside above it.
And the meaning? Guides to Mull translate the Gaelic name as beach of the meadow, or the meadow beside the bay. Not clear running water.
A popular story says crofters cleared from Mull carried the name to Canada. The record points to Macleod instead.
Ottawa approved the name, and it was confirmed that April. That August, Brisebois quit the force.
There's no Fort Brisebois today. But northwest Calgary has a Brisebois Drive.
A hundred and fifty years later, the name has stuck.
